323.title: Nothing can separate us (Romans 8:31–39)
323.hook: neither death nor life, nor height nor depth
323.howItsDone: Romans 8:31–39 is a reading some families choose for Christian funerals, and some Christians memorize verses 38 and 39 to say in times of fear or loss.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a verse that often gets misquoted. Not all things are good; they're woven. Your line was a good thread in the weave.

Losing someone. Being alone. Getting sick. Failing. Being forgotten. Some fears come as a list. Now suppose a friend on the edge of the bed goes through that list out loud. Naming every one. And after each: no, not even that. That's what Paul does at the end of Romans chapter eight. After the groaning and the weaving, he lists the worst things he can think of, and lets none of them win. Some people who have never opened Romans know these lines from a funeral or a wedding.
screen: `SOME FEARS COME AS A LIST.` → `NAMED ONE AT A TIME.` → `NO, NOT EVEN THAT.`

segments.voice: Paul opens with a question, in the King James Bible: "What shall we then say to these things? If God be for us, who can be against us?" Paul had plenty of enemies; none of them gets the final say. Then a list: "Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? shall tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or peril, or sword?" In another letter Paul lists his own beatings, hunger, cold and shipwreck, so none of this is abstract to him. And tradition says that Christians in Rome would soon face the sword, and that Paul himself died there. So his answer isn't cheap: "Nay, in all these things we are more than conquerors through him that loved us." Not by escaping them. Through them. More than conquerors is one word in Greek, a super-conquering. Then the finale: "For I am persuaded, that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor powers, nor things present, nor things to come, Nor height, nor depth, nor any other creature, shall be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord." He builds it in pairs. Death and life: the two ends of everything. Things present and things to come: all of time. Height and depth: all of space. Then, in case he's missed anything, nor any other creature. Then he stops. There's nothing left on the list.
screen: `IF GOD BE FOR US.` · `TRIBULATION, FAMINE, SWORD.` · `MORE THAN CONQUERORS, THROUGH IT.` · `DEATH, LIFE, HEIGHT, DEPTH: NOTHING.` · then, large: `SHALL BE ABLE TO SEPARATE US FROM THE LOVE OF GOD.`

segments.voice: Read verses thirty-eight and thirty-nine slowly from your screen, out loud if you can, in a whisper if you're not alone, pausing after each pair. When a word touches one of your own fears, stay there for a breath, then read the ending once more: shall be able to separate us from the love of God. If you pray, let these words be your prayer; if you don't, let them be something you heard said over you.
screen: `FOR I AM PERSUADED, THAT NEITHER DEATH, NOR LIFE, NOR ANGELS, NOR PRINCIPALITIES, NOR POWERS, NOR THINGS PRESENT, NOR THINGS TO COME, NOR HEIGHT, NOR DEPTH, NOR ANY OTHER CREATURE, SHALL BE ABLE TO SEPARATE US FROM THE LOVE OF GOD, WHICH IS IN CHRIST JESUS OUR LORD.`

segments.voice: Super-conquering. The one Greek word behind more than conquerors, Paul's answer to his own list of everything that might separate us from God's love.
Your line: no, not even that. Not one fear on the list gets the last word. Day three hundred twenty-three, done.

324.title: Paul's grief (Romans 9–10)
324.hook: Paul aches for his own Jewish people; how beautiful are the feet of those who bring good news
324.howItsDone: Some churches pray for the Jewish people in their regular intercessions, and the Catholic Good Friday liturgy includes a prayer for them; since the Holocaust, some churches read Romans 9–11 with particular care.

segments.voice: Yesterday, super-conquering: neither death nor life. Your line was no, not even that.

Someone gets life-changing news, runs home to share it, and finds their family sees it differently. Nobody stops loving anybody. It just aches. Paul has just written that nothing can separate us from God's love. In the next sentence, the mood drops like a stone. He's thinking about his own family, his own people, the Jewish people. Chapters nine through eleven are Paul wrestling, out loud, with grief and hope at once.
screen: `THE BEST NEWS, AND YOUR FAMILY.` → `THE MOOD DROPS LIKE A STONE.` → `GRIEF AND HOPE AT ONCE.`

segments.voice: Paul writes, in the King James Bible: "That I have great heaviness and continual sorrow in my heart." Continual. Not a passing sadness. He'd almost give up his own place with Christ, he says, if it would help his kinsmen. Then he lists his people's honors: "Who are Israelites; to whom pertaineth the adoption, and the glory, and the covenants, and the giving of the law, and the service of God, and the promises." The patriarchs are theirs, and Jesus himself, Paul says, came from them. He calls them my brethren, my kinsmen, and speaks of his people with love. His grief is that his own people, as a people, have not received Jesus as Messiah, and chapters nine and ten turn it over, painfully, without easy answers. Then in chapter ten he widens the door: there is no difference, he says, between Jew and Greek; the same Lord is rich to all who call on him. But how will anyone hear unless someone is sent? He quotes Isaiah: "How beautiful are the feet of them that preach the gospel of peace, and bring glad tidings of good things!" Not faces, not voices: dusty feet that walked the long road to bring the news. Now something honest. Over the centuries, some Christians used these chapters to look down on Jewish people, and that contempt fed real cruelty. After the Holocaust, the Catholic Church, at the Second Vatican Council, firmly rejected that contempt and said the Jewish people remain dear to God, and a number of Protestant churches have said the same. Churches still differ on how to understand Paul's hope today. But the chapters themselves open with an ache, not a sneer.

segments.voice: Bring to mind Jewish people you know, a synagogue near you, or Jewish communities around the world, some facing real hatred today, and hold them with the love Paul had for his own. If you pray, pray for their peace, their safety and their joy; if you don't, simply wish them well with each breath out. Then think of someone whose feet once brought good news to you, and give thanks for them.
Paul's grief. His continual sorrow for his own people, spoken with love, and the beautiful feet of those who carry good news.
Your line: beautiful feet. Good news needs someone willing to carry it. See you tomorrow.

Paul's anger at the people who turned down his message

325.title: The olive tree (Romans 11)
325.hook: Gentiles are grafted into Israel's olive tree; God's gifts are irrevocable
325.howItsDone: Many Christians speak of the Jewish roots of their faith, and some churches mark this with study of the Hebrew Scriptures, Jewish-Christian dialogue, and reflection on Romans 11 during Holocaust remembrance.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Paul's grief for his own people, spoken with love. Your line was beautiful feet.

Some olive trees on the hillsides of the Holy Land are centuries old: trunks twisted like rope, still bearing fruit. A farmer who wants a better tree doesn't plant a new one. He cuts a branch, fits a new one into the wound, binds it, and waits. That's grafting. The new branch lives on the old root's water and strength. Paul, still wrestling with yesterday's question, says one more thing about his people and the new Gentile believers in Rome, with a tree.
screen: `AN OLIVE TREE, CENTURIES OLD.` → `A NEW BRANCH FITTED INTO THE WOUND.` → `PAUL SAYS IT WITH A TREE.`

segments.voice: Chapter eleven opens with a question, in the King James Bible: "I say then, Hath God cast away his people? God forbid." His answer is no, and he's his own proof: I'm an Israelite too, he says. Then the tree. Israel is a cultivated olive tree, rooted in the promises to Abraham. Some of its natural branches, he says, have been broken off. And Gentile believers, people from the nations, are like shoots from a wild olive, grafted in among the branches, drawing life from the root. Here's the surprise: that's backward. Farmers usually graft a good branch onto a wild root, not a wild branch onto a good one. Paul seems to know it; he calls it contrary to nature. The Gentiles got in by a move no farmer would make. Then he turns to the newcomers in Rome, who may have been getting proud: "Boast not against the branches. But if thou boast, thou bearest not the root, but the root thee." You don't hold up the tree. The tree holds you. Then a line many Christians and Jews in conversation today treasure: "For the gifts and calling of God are without repentance." Without repentance means God doesn't take them back. Paul even hopes the broken branches will be grafted in again, and says that all Israel shall be saved, though Christians differ on what he meant. Then, having thought as hard as he can, Paul stops thinking and starts praising: "O the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and knowledge of God!" At the edge of his argument, he doesn't pretend to have it all figured out. He bows.
screen: `HATH GOD CAST AWAY HIS PEOPLE?` · `A WILD BRANCH, GRAFTED IN.` · `CONTRARY TO NATURE.` · `THE GIFTS OF GOD ARE NOT TAKEN BACK.` · then, large: `THOU BEAREST NOT THE ROOT, BUT THE ROOT THEE.`

segments.voice: Think about where your own faith, your questions, or your sense of right and wrong came from: a grandmother who prayed, a teacher, a congregation, a tradition much older than you that someone carried to you across centuries. Picture those roots under you like the old olive tree's; you didn't grow them, and they're holding you. Name one, and give thanks; if you pray, thank God for them by name.
Wild olive. Paul's picture of the Gentiles, a branch grafted in against nature, drawing life from Israel's cultivated root.
Your line: you don't support the root. Whatever you know, someone carried it to you. That's day three hundred twenty-five.

326.title: A living sacrifice (Romans 12:1–2)
326.hook: offer your bodies; be transformed by the renewing of your mind
326.howItsDone: Some Christians begin the day by offering it to God, and some traditions, such as the Catholic Morning Offering, have set prayers for this; Romans 12:1–2 is often memorized.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the olive tree, and the wild olive grafted in against nature. Your line was you don't support the root.

Sacrifice. The word can bring up something dead: an animal on an altar, smoke going up. Or something given up: the sacrifice fly in baseball, the parent who works two jobs. Something lost so something else can happen. Now put together two words that don't seem to belong: a living sacrifice. For eleven chapters, Paul has talked about what God has done: grace, faith, the Spirit, super-conquering. Now he turns a corner. A small word in his first sentence ties what God has done to how to live. Then he asks for something strange.
screen: `SACRIFICE: SOMETHING DEAD, OR LOST.` → `ELEVEN CHAPTERS OF WHAT GOD HAS DONE.` → `NOW PAUL TURNS A CORNER.`

segments.voice: Here it is, in the King James Bible: "I beseech you therefore, brethren, by the mercies of God, that ye present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable unto God, which is your reasonable service." Start with therefore. Everything Paul asks from here grows out of the mercies of God he's already described. Not do this so God will love you, but God has loved you, therefore. Then bodies. Not just your soul, not just your Sunday: your hands, your feet, your tired back, your Tuesday afternoon. And a living sacrifice: not killed on an altar, but offered and still breathing, going on with ordinary life as a gift. The King James says reasonable service; the Greek can mean the worship that makes sense, or spiritual worship. Translators still argue about it. Then verse two: "And be not conformed to this world: but be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind." Conformed: pressed into a shape, like dough in a mold. Transformed is a different kind of change. The Greek is metamorphousthe; you can hear metamorphosis in it, a caterpillar becoming a butterfly. It's the same word the Gospels use for Jesus on the mountain, when he was transfigured and shone. And it's passive: be transformed. Christians hear that as something God does, not something a person pulls off by effort. The change starts in the renewing of your mind, in what a person thinks about and dwells on. These two verses open the practical chapters that follow: worship that walks out of church on two feet.
screen: `THEREFORE: BECAUSE OF GOD'S MERCIES.` · `YOUR BODY, YOUR TUESDAY.` · `CONFORMED, OR TRANSFORMED.` · `METAMORPHOSIS: THE TRANSFIGURATION WORD.` · then, large: `BE YE TRANSFORMED BY THE RENEWING OF YOUR MIND.`

segments.voice: Picture the rest of your day, hour by hour: the commute, the meetings, the dishes, the kids, the errands, nothing special. Hold it all out in open hands as a gift, not a performance, and feel your feet on the floor and your hands, part of the offering too. If you pray, you can offer the day to God in your own words, or in silence.
Living sacrifice. Not something killed on an altar, but a whole ordinary life, body and all, offered to God as a gift.
Your line: be transformed. Not pressed into a mold, but made new. Day three hundred twenty-six.

327.title: Love without pretending (Romans 12:9–21)
327.hook: rejoice with those who rejoice, weep with those who weep; overcome evil with good
327.howItsDone: Romans 12:9–21 is sometimes read at weddings and taught as a picture of everyday Christian love; some Christians try to live out "overcome evil with good" by answering wrongs with kindness.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a living sacrifice, a whole day offered. Your line was be transformed.

A friend texts: I got the job! And in the chest of the person reading it, just for a second, something can tighten. They wanted that kind of news. They type back: so happy for you!!! with three exclamation points, and they mean it, mostly. Or someone they can't stand has a terrible week, and a small, ugly part of them feels something that isn't quite sympathy. Love is easy to perform. The emojis are right there. Now Paul gets practical: a list of short commands, almost like a text thread. The first one is about pretending.
screen: `I GOT THE JOB!` → `SOMETHING TIGHTENS.` → `LOVE IS EASY TO PERFORM.`

segments.voice: The first line, in the King James Bible: "Let love be without dissimulation." Dissimulation is an old word for pretending. The Greek is anupokritos: without hypocrisy. A hypokrites, in Greek, was an actor, someone speaking from behind a stage mask. Paul's point: let love take off the mask. Then the rapid list. Hate what is evil, hold on to what is good. Outdo one another in showing honor. Be patient in trouble. Keep praying. Share with those in need. Welcome strangers. Then two harder lines: "Rejoice with them that do rejoice, and weep with them that weep." Some readers say the weeping is the easier of the two, and that rejoicing with someone whose good news stings is where the mask really comes off. Then Paul turns to enemies. Bless those who persecute you. Don't pay back evil for evil. If it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men. As much as depends on you, because sometimes it doesn't. Leave vengeance to God. Then, quoting Proverbs: "Therefore if thine enemy hunger, feed him; if he thirst, give him drink: for in so doing thou shalt heap coals of fire on his head." Coals of fire sounds like revenge, but some readers hear it as the burning shame of being treated kindly by someone you've wronged, the kind that might change a heart. Nobody's completely sure where the image comes from. The chapter ends: "Be not overcome of evil, but overcome evil with good." You can hear Jesus's own teaching behind it: love your enemies, bless those who curse you.
screen: `A HYPOCRITE WAS AN ACTOR IN A MASK.` · `REJOICE WITH THEM THAT DO REJOICE.` · `AS MUCH AS LIETH IN YOU.` · `FEED YOUR ENEMY: COALS OF FIRE.` · then, large: `OVERCOME EVIL WITH GOOD.`

segments.voice: Think of someone who has good news right now, a promotion, a baby, a trip, a new love, a win, and if there's a little tightness, notice it honestly; that's all right. Picture their face when they got the news, and let yourself be glad with them, really glad, as if their good news were partly yours. If you pray, you can thank God for their joy, by name.
Anupokritos. Paul's Greek word for love without hypocrisy: no actor's mask, glad with the glad, sad with the sad.
Your line: overcome evil with good. Real love doesn't need a mask. Until tomorrow, friend.

328.title: Owe no one anything (Romans 13:8–14)
328.hook: except to love one another; love is the fulfilling of the law
328.howItsDone: Romans 13:11–14 is a traditional reading for the first Sunday of Advent in some churches, and Christians tell Augustine's conversion story as an example of how a single verse can change a life.

segments.voice: Yesterday, anupokritos, love with the mask off. Your line was overcome evil with good.

Plenty of friendships run on a quiet ledger. The friend who paid for lunch last time, so it's your turn. The neighbor who watched your dog, so you owe them one. The twenty dollars your brother still hasn't paid back. Score gets kept, often without anyone meaning to, and it feels fair. Paul has just been talking about paying what you owe: taxes to whom taxes are due, honor to whom honor is due. Settle up, he says. Then he names the one debt you can never pay off, and says to keep it.
screen: `A LITTLE MENTAL LEDGER.` → `PAY WHAT YOU OWE.` → `THE ONE DEBT YOU CAN'T PAY OFF.`

segments.voice: Here it is, in the King James Bible: "Owe no man any thing, but to love one another: for he that loveth another hath fulfilled the law." Clear every other debt; love stays open. You never get to say: there, I've loved you enough, we're even. An old Christian writer, Origen, put it something like this: the debt of love remains with us always, and we pay it daily and always owe it. Then Paul takes the commandments, don't commit adultery, don't kill, don't steal, don't covet, and says they're all summed up in one line from the law of Moses: love your neighbor as yourself. "Love worketh no ill to his neighbour: therefore love is the fulfilling of the law." Fulfilling in Greek is pleroma, fullness: love fills the law up to the brim. Jesus said much the same when he named the two great commandments. Then Paul looks at the clock. The night is far spent, the day is at hand. Wake up. Cast off the works of darkness, and put on the armor of light. He ends with a line with a famous afterlife: "But put ye on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make not provision for the flesh, to fulfil the lusts thereof." Centuries later, a restless teacher named Augustine sat weeping in a garden in Milan. He heard a child's voice nearby, singing, take up and read. He opened Paul's letters, and his eyes fell on these very lines. A light of peace, he wrote, flooded his heart. He tells the story himself, in his Confessions.
screen: `THE ONE DEBT THAT STAYS OPEN.` · `LOVE YOUR NEIGHBOR AS YOURSELF.` · `PLEROMA: FILLED TO THE BRIM.` · `TAKE UP AND READ: AUGUSTINE.` · then, large: `LOVE IS THE FULFILLING OF THE LAW.`

segments.voice: Scan your life for something you owe, a borrowed book, five dollars, a thank-you note, a reply you've put off, a call to someone who always calls you first, and pick the smallest real one and decide when you'll pay it. Then picture someone you love and notice how much you still owe them in love, and owe it gladly. If you pray, you can give thanks for that debt.
Pleroma. The Greek word for fullness: love fills the law up to the brim, the one debt that never closes.
Your line: love fulfils the law. It's the one debt worth keeping open. Day three hundred twenty-eight, done.

329.title: The weak and the strong (Romans 14–15:7)
329.hook: don't quarrel over food and days; welcome one another
329.howItsDone: Christians often turn to Romans 14 when churches disagree over food, holy days, alcohol or worship styles, and some congregations use Romans 15:7 as a motto for hospitality.

segments.voice: Yesterday, pleroma, the one debt that stays open. Your line was love fulfils the law.

Thanksgiving dinner. One cousin is vegan now. An uncle keeps making jokes about it. Someone won't eat before grace; someone else has already started. One sister wants the holiday at church, another at the football game. Nobody is doing anything evil. But by dessert, three people aren't speaking. The church in Rome had its own version of this table. Some believers kept careful rules about food and holy days. Others ate anything and treated every day alike. And they judged each other. Paul, near the end of his letter, sits down at that table.
screen: `A THANKSGIVING TABLE.` → `NOBODY'S DOING ANYTHING EVIL.` → `ROME HAD ITS OWN TABLE.`

segments.voice: Paul starts, in the King James Bible: "Him that is weak in the faith receive ye, but not to doubtful disputations." Welcome them, but not to argue. He calls one group weak, those whose conscience holds them to careful rules about food and days, and the other strong, those who feel free. Paul counts himself among the strong. But notice where he puts the weight. The strong mustn't look down on the weak. The weak mustn't judge the strong. And whoever's freedom might trip up a brother or sister should be willing to set it aside. "One man esteemeth one day above another: another esteemeth every day alike. Let every man be fully persuaded in his own mind." Each one answers to God, not to the person across the table. Paul zooms out: "For the kingdom of God is not meat and drink; but righteousness, and peace, and joy in the Holy Ghost." The dinner matters less than the people at it. He lands here: "Wherefore receive ye one another, as Christ also received us to the glory of God." Receive in Greek is proslambanesthe, to take someone to yourself, to welcome them in. The model isn't tolerance through gritted teeth. It's the way Christ received us. Christians still argue about what counts as a food-and-days question and what's more central, and churches draw that line in different places; some point to this passage to keep a wide table. A week of Romans up close: super-conquering, Paul's grief, the olive tree, a living sacrifice, love without a mask, the debt of love. It all comes down to sitting at one table together.
screen: `RECEIVE THE WEAK, NOT TO ARGUE.` · `EACH ANSWERS TO GOD.` · `NOT MEAT AND DRINK, BUT PEACE AND JOY.` · `AS CHRIST ALSO RECEIVED US.` · then, large: `RECEIVE YE ONE ANOTHER.`

segments.voice: Picture someone who practices, eats, votes, worships or celebrates differently from you, in a way that sometimes gets under your skin, and notice any small judgment that rises, without feeding it. Then imagine pulling out a chair for them at your table, not to fix them, just to welcome them, and meaning it. If you pray, pray for them by name, and for yourself.
Proslambanesthe. Paul's Greek word for receive: to take someone fully to yourself, the way Christ received us at the table.
Your line: welcome one another. There's room for everyone at the table. See you tomorrow.

original.note: Greek: receive, welcome, take someone to yourself.

trapdoor: what you thought: the weak and the strong means weak people and strong people.
what it means: two groups in the Roman church, one keeping food laws and holy days, one feeling free, both told to stop judging and welcome each other.

what a scholar hears: some scholars link the weak to Jewish-background believers and the strong to Gentiles, perhaps after Jews expelled under Claudius returned to Rome, though the evidence is debated.
